Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Trade name: Lamictal

It is one of the most widely prescribed antiepileptics in treatment of focal seizures

it was first used in 1990 in Ireland to treat epilepsy

Mechanism of action

It blocks voltage gated sodium channels (similar to most of the first Gen antiepileptics)

It also inhibit the presynaptic release of glutamate and aspartate

Therapeutic uses

It is effective in treatment of focal seizures (same with the carbamazepine)

It is also effective against idiopathic generalized onset tonic clonic seizures and Lennox Gastaut syndrome

It is also effective in treatment of Absence seizures (but not as effective as ethosuximide or valproate)

Preferred in pregnancy due to low teratogenic potential

It used off label in treatment of bipolar disorder, fibromyalgia, schizophrenia and depression

Adverse effects

Lamotrigine is generally well tolerated but it may lead to:

Headache

Nausea and vomiting

CNS: diplopia

Skin rash (allergic) and rarely progresses to SJS (higher risk if combined with valproic acid)

Insomnia (most antiepileptics cause sedation instead)

Pharmacokinetics

Lamotrigine is well absorbed with bioavailability of 98%

Distribution: binds to proteins by 55%, the rest is distributed to the tissues especially the brain where it exert its effects, Vd is 1.2

It is metabolized by glucuronidation in the liver and excreted in urine

Eliminated by first order kinetics and Half life is around 24 hours

Drug interactions

Lamotrigine is commonly combined with valproate, valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism leading to increase of its drug levels and half life

So lamotrigine dose should be reduced if combined with valproate
